subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_description: Students measure the length of their classroom table using their own handspans and record their counts. Results are compared across the group. The variation in counts for the same object surfaces the core tension: a measurement needs both a number and a reliable unit.

roles.role_description: Each student measures the table with their handspan, records the count, and compares their result with classmates.
Prompts students to notice the variation in counts and asks why five people measuring the same table get five different numbers.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the table measurement challenge and each student measures the table length using their handspan, recording their count.
All counts are written on the board; students observe the spread of numbers and propose reasons for the variation.
Students discuss in pairs what two things every measurement must include (a number and a unit) and what makes a unit reliable or unreliable.
Class shares conclusions; teacher formalises the idea that body-part units vary person to person and cannot serve as shared standards.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening unit, and its job is to let the problem of unreliable units emerge from students' own data rather than from explanation. Watch for the common assumption that measuring is just counting — students may not spontaneously notice that the size of the unit matters as much as the count. A useful checkpoint: can every student articulate both parts of a measurement (number + unit) before you close?

periods.activity_title: From Handspan to SI: Why the World Agreed
periods.activity_description: Students learn how independent measurement systems across regions created trade and communication confusion, leading to the adoption of SI units. The metre is established as the SI unit for length, with its sub-units (cm, mm) and the larger unit km introduced through the conversion relationships.

roles.role_description: Presents the historical problem of incompatible systems and walks students through the SI framework, unit relationships, and the metre's sub-divisions.
Record the unit relationships and complete a structured set of conversion exercises in their notebooks.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the handspan problem from the previous unit, then narrates how differing regional systems caused confusion in trade and travel.
SI units are introduced; the metre is established as the base unit for length; students write the conversion chain 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm.
Students work individually on a set of conversion problems — expressing a given length in different units — and then check answers with a neighbour.
Teacher closes by noting that ancient Indian units such as angula, dhanusa, and yojana served local needs, then connects this to why a universal system became necessary.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's discovery that body-part units are unreliable, this unit explains the institutional solution. A frequent error is confusing the direction of conversion — students multiply when they should divide or vice versa; asking them to check whether their converted answer is a bigger or smaller number than the original is a quick self-correction strategy. The historical note about Indian units is a brief enrichment, not the main thread.

periods.activity_title: Using a Scale Correctly — Three Rules in Practice
periods.activity_description: Students measure a set of everyday objects (comb, pen, pencil, eraser) using a 15-cm scale, deliberately practising correct placement, eye alignment to eliminate parallax, and the broken-scale method. They record readings and compare results with a classmate to assess residual variation.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates each of the three correct techniques — flat placement, vertical eye position, broken-scale reference — before students practise independently.
Measure each object using the correct technique, record readings, and explain to a partner which technique they used for each object and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates all three techniques on a single object, explicitly showing what goes wrong when the scale is tilted, the eye is off-centre, or the zero end is broken.
Students independently measure the comb, pen, pencil, and eraser, recording each reading with the unit; they use the broken-scale method for at least one measurement.
Students compare their readings with a partner and explain any differences; teacher circulates to address parallax errors still appearing.
Brief whole-class check: teacher asks which technique matters most for short objects versus longer ones, and why.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from knowing the units to applying measurement skill, building on the SI framework from the previous unit. The most persistent error here is parallax — students believe they are looking straight down but are not; having them describe their eye position aloud before reading helps catch this. A useful checkpoint is whether students can articulate the broken-scale calculation as a subtraction, not just as a procedure they followed.

periods.activity_title: Measuring What a Ruler Cannot Follow
periods.activity_description: Students investigate how to measure the length of a curved line or surface, choosing between a flexible tape and the thread-and-scale method. They apply whichever method is appropriate to measure curved paths drawn on paper and the circumference of a cylindrical object, then justify their choice.

roles.role_description: Each group selects a method for each curved object, measures it, records the result, and prepares a one-sentence justification for their choice of method.
Poses the problem of measuring a curved string-light decoration as an entry point and circulates to ask groups why a rigid ruler cannot be used directly on a curved path.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Anish's curved verandah decoration scenario as a problem: how do you measure a length that a ruler cannot lie flat along?
Groups measure a curved path drawn on paper and the circumference of a cylindrical object using either thread-and-scale or flexible tape, recording results and method chosen.
Groups share results and compare: did different methods for the same object give the same answer? Students discuss where differences came from.
Class agrees on a rule for when each method is most appropriate; teacher formalises the two methods.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised straight-scale technique in the previous unit, students now encounter the constraint of curved surfaces — a natural extension of the same measurement skill. Watch for groups who stretch the thread tight rather than following the curve faithfully; this is the most common source of underestimation. A good probing question: 'If you stretch the thread a little, does your answer get bigger or smaller than the real length, and why?'
materials: Paper with curved paths drawn on it

periods.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
periods.activity_title: Why Distances Disagree: The Reference Point Discovery
periods.activity_description: Students examine the scenario of Deepa and her friends disagreeing about which place is closer, then discover through diagram analysis that each child is measuring from a different starting point. They identify that a shared reference point is essential for distances to be compared meaningfully.

roles.role_description: Presents the Deepa scenario and draws a diagram on the board showing each child's house and the two destinations, asking students to identify what is different about each child's measurement.
Sketch their own version of the scenario, mark each child's reference point, and write a sentence explaining why the children's distance claims all differ even though they are all correct.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the scenario: Deepa and friends each say a different place is closer to school; students read the scenario and form an initial opinion on who is right.
Students sketch a simple map of the scenario, marking each child's house and the school and garden, then identify from whose house each distance is measured.

Class discussion: students explain how all the children can be simultaneously correct, and what a reference point is — a fixed object or point from which all distances in a comparison must be calculated.
Teacher reinforces with the Kabaddi court and kilometre-stone examples; students record a definition of reference point in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens a new part of the chapter — from measuring length to describing position — and it is worth briefly linking back to the idea of a standard starting mark on a scale (the zero-mark or chosen centimetre) as a small-scale reference point. The central misconception to watch here is that students may think only one child is right; the key insight is that all can be correct from their own reference point, and that is exactly why a shared reference point is necessary. The Kabaddi court example is a strong concrete anchor if the abstract definition feels slippery.

periods.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
periods.activity_title: Motion, Rest, and the Role of the Observer
periods.activity_description: Students investigate the bus scenario in which Deepa observes her fellow passengers and a building outside. They determine whether each object is in motion or at rest by specifying a reference point, discovering that motion and rest are not absolute properties of an object but depend on the chosen reference.

roles.role_description: Each group analyses the bus scenario for two reference points (Deepa inside the bus; a building outside) and decides, with justification, whether the passengers are in motion or at rest for each reference.
Facilitates a structured discussion in which groups present their findings and the class reconciles apparently contradictory answers by identifying the reference point each answer assumes.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the bus scenario; each group receives a two-column table listing 'passengers' and 'building' against 'reference: Deepa' and 'reference: building outside'.
Groups fill in the table, writing 'at rest' or 'in motion' with a one-sentence justification for each cell.
Groups share their completed tables; class identifies any cells where different groups disagreed and resolves the disagreement by naming the reference point.
Teacher formalises the definition: an object is in motion if its position changes with respect to the reference point over time; otherwise it is at rest.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who completed the reference-point discovery in the previous unit are now applying that concept to classify motion — a direct cognitive step up. The pervasive misconception here is that motion is an intrinsic property of an object ('the passengers are moving because the bus is moving'); the activity is designed to surface and correct this by forcing students to name a reference point before making any claim. A group that writes contradictory answers in the two columns has understood the concept better than one that writes consistent answers without explaining why.
materials: Printed or hand-drawn two-column scenario table

periods.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
periods.activity_description: Students construct two simple apparatus — a thread-and-eraser whirl and a pendulum — and observe the path each traces. They record path descriptions and classify each as circular or oscillatory, identifying the defining feature of each type.

roles.role_description: Each group makes a whirl (eraser on thread, swung in a horizontal circle) and a pendulum (eraser displaced slightly and released), observes and sketches the path of each, and records the defining feature that determines its classification.
Demonstrates safe whirling before students begin, monitors for safety, and asks each group to describe the fixed point about which the pendulum swings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the whirl (safely, with adequate space) and the pendulum setup, naming the two motion types to be explored: circular and oscillatory.
Groups construct both apparatus, observe each in action, sketch the path traced, and note whether the object returns to a fixed position and repeats its path.
Groups write a classification card for each apparatus: the type of motion, the defining feature (circular path; to-and-fro about a fixed position), and one example from daily life.
Two groups share their classification cards; class checks that both types are defined by path, not speed or size.

periods.teacher_notes: Having defined motion in the previous unit, students now classify it by examining the path — a natural next step. A common confusion is between circular and oscillatory motion: students may describe a pendulum as 'going in a circle' because it curves; emphasise that circular motion traces a complete closed circle whereas oscillatory motion goes back and forth about a fixed position. A probing question: 'Could the pendulum ever reach the other side without coming back? What does that tell you about the path?'
materials: Pencil or clamp stand to anchor pendulum

periods.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
periods.activity_title: Linear Motion and the Vibrating Strip
periods.activity_description: Students examine linear motion examples from the chapter — dropped eraser, marching students, box pushed across floor — and then observe a thin metal strip clamped at one end and pressed at the free end. They determine whether the strip's motion is linear or oscillatory and construct a complete three-type classification of motion with defining features.

roles.role_description: Clamps or holds the metal strip, demonstrates its vibration, and guides students to compare the strip's motion to the pendulum from the previous unit.

Observe the strip, classify its motion with a justification, then independently construct a three-column summary table for linear, circular, and oscillatory motion with one defining feature and two examples each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the linear motion examples from the chapter and elicits from students what they all have in common (straight-line path); students add this to their notes.
Teacher demonstrates the vibrating strip; students observe carefully and decide independently whether it is linear, circular, or oscillatory, writing a justification before any class discussion.
Students construct a three-column classification table (motion type | defining feature | two examples) drawing on all activities from this and the previous unit.
Two or three students share their tables; class checks that defining features are about path, and that each example is correctly matched.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit introduced circular and oscillatory motion through hands-on apparatus; this unit completes the three-type classification by adding linear motion and the vibrating strip. Watch for students who classify the vibrating strip as circular because it bends — the key distinction is that it moves to and fro about a fixed rest position, not along a complete closed circle. The three-column table is a productive consolidation task and doubles as a reference the students will use in the next unit.
materials: Thin metal strip (ruler or hacksaw blade)
Clamp or heavy book to anchor one end

periods.stage_label: Measure accurately and classify motion by applying both competencies together
periods.activity_title: Park Motion Survey: Measure, Observe, Classify
periods.activity_description: Students work from a description of a children's park containing swings, a slide, a merry-go-round, and a seesaw. They measure a given scale-diagram distance to determine a path length, then classify the motion of each piece of equipment with a justification, applying both accurate-measurement and motion-classification reasoning simultaneously.

roles.role_description: Each group uses a scale diagram of the park to measure a marked path length using the thread-and-scale method, then classifies the motion of each piece of equipment with a written justification referencing path type.
Distributes the park diagram, specifies the scale ratio, and circulates to prompt groups who are classifying by speed or by visible back-and-forth without identifying the path type precisely.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the park diagram, explains the scale, and sets the dual task: measure one marked curved path on the diagram and classify each piece of equipment's motion.
Groups measure the marked path using thread and ruler, convert the scale reading to real-world units, then complete a classification table for each piece of equipment with justifications.
Groups compare path length answers and reconcile any differences by checking thread placement; they then share two or three motion classifications and defend them against the class.
Teacher signals the integrated insight: the same skills of careful measurement and reference-based classification work together whenever we describe how objects move through space.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together both central threads of the chapter — accurate measurement technique and motion classification — by placing them in a single task. A common slip is students classifying the seesaw as oscillatory and the slide as linear without examining the path carefully; ask groups to describe the path traced by a person riding each, not just the equipment's overall shape. If a group's path-length measurement differs noticeably from others, use that as an opportunity to revisit the thread-alignment technique from the earlier unit on curved measurement.
materials: Printed scale diagram of a children's park (one per group)

periods.stage_label: Measure accurately and classify motion by applying both competencies together
periods.activity_description: Student groups design and solve a short measurement-and-classification challenge of their own: they select an object in the classroom, measure a relevant length using the most appropriate technique, determine the object's type of motion with a reference point stated explicitly, and present their complete reasoning to the class.

roles.role_description: Each group selects an object, chooses and applies the correct measurement technique, identifies a reference point, classifies the motion with justification, and presents their reasoning in a structured two-minute summary.
Facilitates group selection to ensure different motion types are covered across groups, and during presentations asks probing questions about why a particular measurement technique was chosen.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the challenge parameters: each group selects an object, plans their measurement approach, and identifies which motion type they expect to demonstrate; groups spend this time planning.

Groups carry out their measurement, record their reference point, classify the motion, and prepare a brief structured summary (object | measurement method | length | reference point | motion type | justification).
Each group delivers a short presentation of their summary; the class checks the justification against the path-based classification criteria developed across the chapter.

Teacher draws the chapter to a close by connecting the opening handspan problem to the final presentations: measurement has grown from informal body-part units to precise SI technique applied alongside a principled account of motion.

periods.teacher_notes: In the previous unit students applied both skills together with a structured diagram; here they direct their own investigation, which requires them to choose their tools and justify their choices — the highest demand of the chapter. Watch for groups that name a motion type without stating a reference point; at this stage every motion claim should name both the path type and the reference relative to which the object is observed to move. The closing two-unit connection to the chapter's beginning is intentional and worth making explicit to the students.
materials: Various classroom objects (door, pendulum, fan if available, etc.)

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure with handspans to discover why informal units fail, then learn SI units and practice length conversions.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why body-part units produce different measurements for the same object and correctly express a given length using SI units and their conversion relationships.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students practise correct scale placement, parallax elimination, and the broken-scale method for straight objects, then apply thread-and-scale and flexible-tape methods to curved lengths.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can accurately measure the length of both straight and curved objects using the correct instrument and technique, and can identify and correct common measurement errors.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discover that position and distance comparisons require a shared reference point, then apply this to classify whether objects are in motion or at rest relative to a specified reference.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the reference point in a given scenario, explain why the same object can be simultaneously at rest and in motion relative to different references, and use that reasoning to define motion.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe and construct whirling-eraser, pendulum, and vibrating-strip apparatus, classify each as circular, oscillatory, or linear by identifying the path traced, and build a three-type classification framework.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify the motion of an object as linear, circular, or oscillatory by describing the path it traces and justify each classification with a path-based criterion.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Measure accurately and classify motion by applying both competencies together
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students apply accurate SI measurement technique and reference-point-based motion classification simultaneously in a park-diagram task and a self-directed investigation.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can measure the length of a straight or curved path using the appropriate SI technique and describe or classify the motion of objects by specifying a reference point and identifying the path traced, reasoning across both skills in an integrated task.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why body-part units produce different measurements for the same object and correctly express a given length using SI units and their conversion relationships.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: Five students measure the length of the same table using their handspans and each gets a different count. What is the most direct reason the counts differ?

options.label: A
options.text: Each student's handspan is a different size, so the unit of measurement is different each time.

options.label: B
options.text: The students did not start from the same end of the table.

options.label: C
options.text: Handspans can only be used to measure curved surfaces, not flat ones.

options.label: D
options.text: The table length changes slightly each time it is measured.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on procedural error (starting point) rather than recognising that the unit itself varies — conflates technique error with unit-size variation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student holds a misconception that handspans have a domain restriction, not understanding that the problem is unit variability, not surface type.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student attributes measurement variation to the object changing rather than to the unit varying — does not yet grasp that the unit is the source of inconsistency.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to articulate the reason in writing can demonstrate this outcome verbally by comparing two classmates' handspans and explaining the consequence. Visual learners may benefit from seeing two differently sized handspan cut-outs next to the same drawn line.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why body-part units produce different measurements for the same object and correctly express a given length using SI units and their conversion relationships.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A pencil is 85 mm long. What is its length in centimetres?

options.label: A
options.text: 8.5 cm

options.label: B
options.text: 850 cm

options.label: D
options.text: 85 cm

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student multiplied by 10 instead of dividing — confuses the direction of conversion between mm and cm.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student divided by 100 instead of 10 — confuses the mm-to-cm relationship with the cm-to-m relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student dropped the conversion entirely and treated the numeric value as already in centimetres — does not apply the 1 cm = 10 mm relationship.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who lose track of conversion direction benefit from writing the relationship 1 cm = 10 mm and asking whether centimetres are larger or smaller than millimetres before computing. Oral explanation of the conversion chain is an equally valid demonstration pathway.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can accurately measure the length of both straight and curved objects using the correct instrument and technique, and can identify and correct common measurement errors.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student places a ruler along a pen and reads the length by looking at the ruler from a slight angle rather than directly above. How will this affect the measurement and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The reading will be incorrect because the line of sight is not perpendicular to the scale, causing a parallax error.

options.label: B
options.text: The reading will be unaffected because the ruler's markings do not change when viewed from an angle.

options.label: C
options.text: The reading will be incorrect because the ruler bends slightly when the eye is not directly above it.

options.label: D
options.text: The reading will be incorrect because viewing from an angle changes the actual length of the pen.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student believes angle of viewing is irrelevant — has not connected the concept of parallax to measurement accuracy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student knows viewing angle causes an error but attributes it to physical bending of the ruler rather than to the line-of-sight displacement that produces parallax.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates an observation error with a change in the physical object — a significant misconception about what measurement is recording.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot articulate 'parallax' by name can still demonstrate the outcome by describing what they see change when they shift their head — accept functional descriptions. Demonstrating with a physical ruler and asking students to read from two positions is an accessible alternative pathway.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can accurately measure the length of both straight and curved objects using the correct instrument and technique, and can identify and correct common measurement errors.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to measure the girth of a tree trunk. Which instrument and method should they use, and why is a rigid 15-cm scale unsuitable?

options.label: A
options.text: A flexible measuring tape, because it can follow the curved surface; a rigid scale cannot bend to follow the curve and would only measure a straight chord across the trunk.

options.label: B
options.text: A rigid scale, because the millimetre markings on it are more accurate than those on a tape.

options.label: C
options.text: A flexible measuring tape, because rigid scales are only accurate for lengths greater than 15 cm.

options.label: D
options.text: A thread measured against a rigid scale is wrong here; only a flexible tape gives accurate results for any curved surface.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses precision of markings with suitability for the measurement task — focuses on graduation size rather than ability to follow a curved surface.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student identifies the correct instrument but invents an incorrect length-based rule for the rigid scale's limitation rather than the curvature-based reason.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student incorrectly rejects the thread-and-scale method, which is also valid; this reveals confusion between two acceptable methods for curved measurement.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate this outcome by physically trying to lay a rigid ruler against a cylindrical object and describing what they observe, without needing to produce a written explanation. Sketching the chord versus the arc is an alternative mode of justification.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can accurately measure the length of both straight and curved objects using the correct instrument and technique, and can identify and correct common measurement errors.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student's scale is damaged at both ends: the zero mark is worn away and the 14 cm mark is also unclear. The student aligns one end of a pencil with the 1.0 cm mark and the other end falls at 13.4 cm. What is the length of the pencil? Show your reasoning.
expected_elements: States that the length is found by subtracting the smaller reading from the larger reading (13.4 cm − 1.0 cm).
Explains why the zero mark not being used does not matter (any clear reference mark can serve as the starting point).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who cannot write the full calculation can draw the ruler with the two positions marked and write only the subtraction step — the physical reasoning is equivalent. Verbal explanation accepted in place of written working.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the reference point in a given scenario, explain why the same object can be simultaneously at rest and in motion relative to different references, and use that reasoning to define motion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: Deepa is sitting in a moving bus. Her friend Anish is standing on the footpath watching the bus go by. Which statement correctly describes Deepa's motion?

options.label: A
options.text: Deepa is at rest relative to the bus seat and in motion relative to Anish on the footpath.

options.label: B
options.text: Deepa is in motion relative to the bus seat because the bus engine is running.

options.label: C
options.text: Deepa is at rest in all cases because she is not physically moving her body.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether Deepa is in motion depends only on her speed, not on any reference point.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the engine being on (cause of bus movement) with Deepa's position relative to the bus changing — does not apply the definition of motion as a change of position relative to a reference.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student defines motion by bodily activity rather than by change of position relative to a reference point — a persistent everyday misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student substitutes speed for the reference-point criterion — conflates the measure of motion with the condition for defining it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate this outcome by acting it out: one student sits still while a partner walks past, and both describe each other's motion from their own reference. Oral description is a valid alternative to written response.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the reference point in a given scenario, explain why the same object can be simultaneously at rest and in motion relative to different references, and use that reasoning to define motion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A kilometre stone on the road to Delhi reads '120 km'. What is the reference point for this distance, and what does the reading tell a traveller?

options.label: A
options.text: The reference point is Delhi; the traveller is 120 km away from Delhi along this road.

options.label: B
options.text: The reference point is the traveller's starting city; the stone shows distance already covered.

options.label: C
options.text: The reference point is the stone itself; all distances on the road are measured from that stone.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no reference point; the stone simply marks the 120th kilometre of the road from its beginning.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student assumes the reference is the traveller's personal origin rather than the fixed destination stated on the stone — shows that the concept of a shared fixed reference has not fully replaced the idea of a personal origin.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the kilometre stone (the sign) with the reference point — does not distinguish between a marker and the reference from which distances are measured.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student treats the road's starting point as an implicit reference but denies that a reference point exists — partially correct but misidentifies what constitutes a reference point.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with kilometre stones can demonstrate the same outcome using the Kabaddi court example from the chapter — both involve a fixed reference from which all markings are made.

assessment_items.stage_label: Identify and use a reference point to describe position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the reference point in a given scenario, explain why the same object can be simultaneously at rest and in motion relative to different references, and use that reasoning to define motion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: Padma says the library is closer to school than the park is. Tasneem says the park is closer. Both are correct. Explain how this is possible, naming the reference point each child is using.
expected_elements: States that Padma and Tasneem are measuring from different reference points (their own houses or locations).
Explains that distance comparisons are only meaningful when made from the same reference point.
Names a specific reference point for each child (e.g., Padma's house is closer to the library; Tasneem's house is closer to the park).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult can draw a simple sketch showing both houses and the two destinations, marking distances, as an equivalent demonstration. Pair discussion before individual writing supports students who need to talk through the logic.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the motion of an object as linear, circular, or oscillatory by describing the path it traces and justify each classification with a path-based criterion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: An eraser is tied to a thread and whirled in a horizontal circle. A separate eraser is attached to a thread, displaced slightly from its rest position, and released as a pendulum. Which row correctly matches each motion to its type?

options.label: A
options.text: Whirling eraser: circular motion; pendulum eraser: oscillatory motion.

options.label: B
options.text: Whirling eraser: oscillatory motion; pendulum eraser: circular motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Whirling eraser: circular motion; pendulum eraser: circular motion.

options.label: D
options.text: Whirling eraser: linear motion; pendulum eraser: oscillatory motion.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student reverses the two classifications — likely confuses the curved arc of the pendulum with a circle and the rotational feel of whirling with back-and-forth.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies the whirling eraser but over-applies 'circular' to the pendulum because it also moves in a curved arc — does not distinguish a complete closed circle from a to-and-fro arc.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student incorrectly classifies the whirling eraser as linear — may be focusing on the straight thread rather than the circular path traced by the eraser.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can trace each path on paper first — a circle for the whirl and an arc back and forth for the pendulum — and then classify from the drawing. Physical demonstration with actual apparatus is equally valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the motion of an object as linear, circular, or oscillatory by describing the path it traces and justify each classification with a path-based criterion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A thin metal strip is clamped at one end. The free end is pressed down and released. What type of motion does the free end show, and what is the defining feature that determines this classification?

options.label: A
options.text: Oscillatory motion; the free end moves to and fro about a fixed rest position.

options.label: B
options.text: Circular motion; the free end traces a curved path as it bends.

options.label: C
options.text: Linear motion; the free end moves in a straight line when pressed down.

options.label: D
options.text: Oscillatory motion; the free end moves faster than the clamped end.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on the curved shape of the bending strip and over-generalises 'curved path' to mean circular — does not distinguish a closed circular path from a bending arc that reverses direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student focuses on the downward press action (which is linear) rather than on the subsequent to-and-fro motion of the free end after release.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly names oscillatory motion but justifies it with speed difference between ends rather than the path-based criterion (to-and-fro about a fixed position) — shows partial understanding.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate this by pressing and releasing a flexible ruler clamped to a desk edge and verbally describing what the tip does — physical observation substitutes for the written classification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify motion by path and justify with evidence
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify the motion of an object as linear, circular, or oscillatory by describing the path it traces and justify each classification with a path-based criterion.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says that both a merry-go-round and a pendulum show 'repeated motion' and so they must be the same type. Do you agree? Explain your answer by describing the path each object traces.
expected_elements: States that the merry-go-round traces a complete closed circular path — circular motion.
States that the pendulum moves to and fro about a fixed rest position without completing a full circle — oscillatory motion.
Identifies that 'repeated motion' alone is not enough to determine the type; the shape of the path is the defining criterion.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write the argument can draw the two paths side by side (a full circle and a back-and-forth arc) and annotate them — the drawn comparison is an equivalent demonstration of path-based classification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure accurately and classify motion by applying both competencies together
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure the length of a straight or curved path using the appropriate SI technique and describe or classify the motion of objects by specifying a reference point and identifying the path traced, reasoning across both skills in an integrated task.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student measures the curved path of a swing's arc using a thread, then lays the thread on a ruler and reads 24.0 cm on a scale diagram. The scale of the diagram is 1 cm represents 50 cm. What is the actual length of the arc, and which type of motion does the swing show?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual arc length is 1200 cm; the swing shows oscillatory motion.

options.label: B
options.text: Actual arc length is 1200 cm; the swing shows circular motion because the arc is curved.

options.label: C
options.text: Actual arc length is 24 cm; the scale conversion is not needed because the thread already gives the real length.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual arc length is 0.48 cm; the swing shows oscillatory motion.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student applies the scale conversion correctly but misclassifies the swing as circular because the arc is curved — confuses a curved arc with a complete circular path; does not integrate path-type criterion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student measures the diagram correctly but does not apply the scale conversion — treats the diagram measurement as the real-world measurement; also conflates the diagram and the actual object.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student divides instead of multiplies in the scale conversion — reverses the direction of the scale ratio; correctly classifies the motion type.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who lose track of the scale conversion can write out '1 cm on diagram = 50 cm real' and use repeated addition rather than multiplication; both arrive at the same answer. Students who need support with the motion classification can refer to their three-column classification table from the earlier units.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure the length of a straight or curved path using the appropriate SI technique and describe or classify the motion of objects by specifying a reference point and identifying the path traced, reasoning across both skills in an integrated task.

assessment_items.question_text: Hardeep stands on the footpath and watches a merry-go-round spin in the park. He then climbs on and sits on one of the seats. How does the description of the seat's motion change between these two situations, and what explains the change?

options.label: A
options.text: When Hardeep is on the footpath, the seat is in motion relative to him; when he sits on the seat, the seat is at rest relative to him — the reference point changed.

options.label: B
options.text: When Hardeep is on the footpath, the seat is in motion; when he sits on it, it is still in motion because the merry-go-round keeps spinning.

options.label: C
options.text: When Hardeep sits on the seat, the seat stops being in motion because a person's weight slows the merry-go-round.

options.label: D
options.text: The seat is always in circular motion regardless of where Hardeep stands, so the description does not change.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies the motion from the footpath but does not apply the reference-point concept when Hardeep moves to the seat — treats motion as absolute rather than relative.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student attributes the change in motion description to a physical cause (weight) rather than to a change in reference point — confuses a physical effect with a conceptual shift in perspective.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student treats motion type (circular) as fixed and absolute, ignoring the distinction between the type of path and the question of relative motion with respect to a chosen reference.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can act this out with two classmates — one staying still and one riding a spinning chair — and describe each other's motion from each vantage point before writing. This embodied experience directly demonstrates the reference-point dependence.

assessment_items.question_text: Rehan wants to know whether the string of lights decorating a curved archway in his school is long enough to reach from one pillar to another in a straight line. Describe, step by step, how Rehan should measure the length of the curved string and the straight-line distance between the pillars, state which measurement will be greater and why, and explain what this tells Rehan about whether the string is long enough.
look_for: Describes a correct method for measuring the curved string length (flexible tape or thread-and-scale), including the key step of following the curve faithfully.
Describes a correct method for measuring the straight-line distance between the pillars (rigid ruler or metre scale placed flat).
States that the curved string measurement will be greater than the straight-line distance, and explains that a curved path between two points is always longer than the straight line joining them.
Concludes correctly that the string is long enough to span the straight distance because its actual length (along the curve) is greater.
Uses SI units consistently in the described procedure.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who cannot produce extended prose can answer in numbered steps or a two-column table (what to measure | how to measure it); the logical reasoning in any format is the demonstration. Students who need a concrete anchor can refer to the curved string-light scenario from the chapter.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Equipment | Path traced (describe) | Reference point for 'in motion' | Motion type | How would you measure the path length?
Swing (occupied, moving) | | | | 
Slide (child sliding down) | | | | 
Merry-go-round (child seated, spinning) | | | | 
Seesaw (moving up and down) | | | | 
Child walking from gate to slide | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each piece of equipment or movement in the park: (1) describe the path traced by the moving object or person, (2) name a specific reference point that makes this object 'in motion', (3) classify the motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory, and (4) state which measurement instrument or method you would use to measure the path length and why.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use what you know about how paths look (straight line, closed circle, back and forth) to fill column 2. For column 2 (reference point), name a fixed object in the park. For column 4 (measurement method), choose from: rigid ruler, flexible tape, or thread-and-scale — and give one reason for your choice.
format_of_output: Completed table with all five rows and four columns filled.
One sentence below the table explaining which two pieces of equipment show periodic motion and what 'periodic' means.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's integrated implied LO requires students to simultaneously apply accurate measurement selection and reference-point-based motion classification across multiple objects, which a classification table with justification columns directly and naturally elicits.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can describe a path, anchor a motion claim to a named reference point, classify by path type, and select a measurement instrument with a reason — all in one integrated operation, as the final stage's LO requires.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold column headers separate the four sub-operations of the integrated task so the teacher can assess each component independently; a student who fills three columns correctly but errors on one reveals precisely where the integration breaks down.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: paths described in geometric terms (straight line, complete circle, back-and-forth arc); reference points named as specific fixed objects (gate, ground, bench); measurement method choice explicitly linked to path shape. Weak: motion type stated without path description; reference point given as a vague 'something outside'; measurement method chosen by familiarity rather than suitability.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find prose difficult can use single words or short phrases in the table cells — the classification and justification structure is the demonstration, not the prose. Students who need support distinguishing circular from oscillatory can sketch the path in the margin before classifying.
